bridges.description: Infer that God exists from the cumulative case.
Infer a transcendent intelligent creator from cosmic evidence.
Ground objective morality in God’s nature.
Identify the creator through resurrection evidence.
Ground reason and free will in theism.
Infer that God probably does not exist because natural explanations are likelier.
Prefer testable natural explanations for cosmic and miracle claims.
Explain morality through evolution, empathy, and humanism.
Explain mind and religious belief through brains.
Create meaning through present human relationships.

sections.title: Cosmological origins and fine-tuning
sections.rationale: This section receives 22 percent because cosmic beginning and fine-tuning are two direct pro routes to a creator, answered by observer selection, causal consistency, and explicit cosmological uncertainty.

sections.title: Miracles, resurrection, and historical evidence
sections.rationale: This section receives 24 percent because resurrection is Turek’s only specifically Christian identification of God and Nørmark contests its testimony, probability, literary form, and historical method through four independently assessable replies.

sections.title: Morality, humanism, and violence
sections.rationale: This section receives 23 percent because both speakers repeatedly use moral grounding, empathy, humanism, and ideological violence to test whether God is needed for objective value.

sections.title: Reason, mind, and scientific method
sections.rationale: This section receives 16 percent because method, cognitive explanation, material mind, and free will constrain both worldviews but are less direct than the cosmic, historical, and moral cases.

sections.title: Meaning, redemption, and closing cases
sections.rationale: This section receives 15 percent because redemption and created human meaning state practical consequences and contain both final answers, while largely synthesizing arguments developed elsewhere.
